title: The Diary Is Full. The Vet's Calendar Still Sets the Ceiling on Revenue.
linkedin:
Spring in Australia means kitten season and puppy season land in the same few months, and veterinary practices watch their diary fill out almost overnight.

It feels like growth. It usually isn't, not in the way it looks.

Here's the specific pattern: revenue in a vet practice is capped by clinician hours and theatre time, not by how many clients want an appointment. Once the diary is full, more demand doesn't create more revenue. It just creates a longer waiting list.

There's a lever hiding in plain sight though. Clinical revenue is capped by the vet's calendar. Retail revenue, parasite prevention, prescription diets, dispensed medication, isn't. Once a client is already in the building, a nurse or reception team can grow that side without consuming another minute of clinician time.

The season that fills the diary fastest is also the season most practices under-invest in their retail side, because everyone's attention is on keeping up with consults.

There's a cash timing trap too. Locum cover and surgical consumables for the surge get paid before the matching revenue clears, especially with pet insurers or finance providers in the mix. A fully booked October can still produce a tighter November.

A full diary and a more profitable practice are not automatically the same thing.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.

A note for veterinary practice owners across Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria as spring's kitten and puppy season fills the appointment book.

A fully booked diary feels like a strong quarter, and in most businesses it would be. In a vet practice, revenue is capped by clinician hours and theatre time, not by how many clients want an appointment. Once the calendar is full, extra demand creates a longer waiting list rather than extra income.

There is a part of the practice that can still grow through this season without adding another vet hour: the retail side, parasite prevention, prescription diets and dispensed medication, which only needs a client already in the building rather than more of the vet's time.

Worth watching too is the cash side. Locum cover and surgical supplies bought ahead of the rush are often paid for before the matching revenue clears, so a fully booked month can still leave the bank account tighter than expected the month after.
